prompt: A request for `/static/logo.png` misses at the edge location in Recife. Where does it go next?
hint: There is a tier between the edges and the shop.

choices.text: Straight to the bucket in `sa-east-1`
choices.why: Only a miss at the regional edge cache reaches the origin.

choices.text: To a regional edge cache, shared by several edges
choices.why: Right. A hit there is answered without the origin; only a second miss goes back to the shop.

choices.text: To the next nearest edge location, then the next
choices.why: Edges do not ask each other. Behind each of them sits a regional cache.

choices.text: Back to the viewer, with an error until the edge is filled
choices.why: A miss is fetched, not refused. The viewer waits a little longer and gets the file.

prompt: The bucket `shop-assets` must stay private, and its files must still be served to everybody through the distribution. What makes that work in AWS?
hint: Two halves: one signs, the other agrees.

choices.text: Turning off Block Public Access, so CloudFront can read it
choices.why: That would let anybody read it directly. OAC exists so that nothing has to be made public.

choices.text: Making the bucket a custom origin over HTTPS
choices.why: A custom origin reaches what is public. The bucket stays closed to it.

choices.text: OAC signing the requests, and a policy that trusts only those
choices.why: Right. The condition on `AWS:SourceArn` names the distribution, and a direct request to S3 is refused.

choices.text: A cache policy that keeps the files at the edge forever
choices.why: How long a copy is kept says nothing about who may read the bucket.

prompt: In moto, `get-distribution` shows the bucket origin with `None` where the `OriginAccessControlId` should be. What follows?
hint: The file sent had the id in it.

choices.text: Only that moto 5.2.3 drops the OAC, which AWS would keep
choices.why: Right. The configuration was right; the lab simply does not keep that field, so it cannot show the protection.

choices.text: The OAC was created in the wrong region
choices.why: CloudFront is global, and so is its OAC; there was no region to get wrong.

choices.text: The bucket policy was missing, so the OAC was removed
choices.why: The policy came after, and AWS never removes an OAC for a missing policy; it would simply refuse the reads.

choices.text: The distribution was still `InProgress`
choices.why: A distribution being deployed still returns the configuration it was given.

prompt: The shop's account works in `sa-east-1`. A colleague requests the certificate for `cdn.shop.example.com` in `sa-east-1` and cannot select it in the distribution. Why?
hint: CloudFront looks for certificates in one region only.

choices.text: It has to be validated first, and validation takes a day
choices.why: Validation is needed, but a validated certificate in São Paulo would still not appear.

choices.text: A distribution can only use the default `cloudfront.net` certificate
choices.why: A distribution serves its own names with an ACM certificate; the question is where that certificate lives.

choices.text: CloudFront takes ACM certificates only from `us-east-1`
choices.why: Right. A certificate lives in the region that issued it, and CloudFront reads `us-east-1`'s, wherever the shop runs.

choices.text: The name must first be added as an alias in Route 53
choices.why: The alias record comes after; the certificate list would be empty either way.

prompt: A distribution's own address ends in `___.net`, and that is the name viewers are sent to until an alias is added.
hint: The domain in the transcript, after the random part.

prompt: Where does the CLI show that CloudFront belongs to no region? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three places in the section's transcripts.

choices.text: The `Location` is `cloudfront.amazonaws.com`, with no region in it
choices.why: Right. One address for the whole service.

choices.text: The ARN has an empty region field
choices.why: Right. `arn:aws:cloudfront::123456789012:…`, two colons together.

choices.text: `--region ap-southeast-2` lists the same distribution
choices.why: Right. The region flag changes nothing for a global service.

choices.text: The domain name ends in `sa-east-1.cloudfront.net`
choices.why: It does not: the domain is a random name under `cloudfront.net`, with no region.

choices.text: The ACM certificate was listed in São Paulo
choices.why: It was listed in `us-east-1` and not in São Paulo; ACM is regional, which is the point of that transcript.

prompt: To be safe, a colleague adds the session cookie to the cache key of `/static/*`. What happens to the images?
hint: Everything in the key divides the hit rate.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since images do not read cookies
choices.why: The image does not read it, but the cache does: a different cookie is a different key.

choices.text: One copy per customer, so the cache barely helps
choices.why: Right. One copy per session is no cache at all. A cookie the origin needs goes in an origin request policy instead.

choices.text: The images become private to each customer, which is safer
choices.why: The key decides which copy answers, not who may ask. Privacy is a signed URL's job.

choices.text: CloudFront refuses the policy, since cookies are not allowed in a key
choices.why: Cookies are allowed in a cache key, which is exactly why this mistake is possible.

prompt: Match each managed policy to what it does.
hint: Two cache policies and one origin request policy.

pairs.right: keys on the path and keeps a copy for a day by default
keeps nothing, so every request reaches the origin
forwards every header, cookie and query string to the origin

right_distractors: signs every request to the bucket

prompt: Under `CachingOptimized`, the origin sends a file with no `Cache-Control` header at all. How long may an edge keep it?
hint: The policy has a minimum, a default and a maximum.

choices.text: Not at all: without a header nothing is cached
choices.why: A file that says nothing gets the policy's default, which is not zero here.

choices.text: A year, the policy's maximum
choices.why: The maximum applies when the origin asks for more; a silent file gets the default.

choices.text: A day, the policy's default
choices.why: Right. One second, a day and a year are its minimum, default and maximum.

choices.text: One second, the policy's minimum
choices.why: The minimum stops an origin asking for less; it is not what a silent file gets.

prompt: After a deployment the shop invalidates `/static/css/shop.css`. The invalidation completes, and some customers still see the old styles for hours. Which explanation fits?
hint: Whose caches can CloudFront reach?

choices.text: The invalidation needs a wildcard to reach every edge
choices.why: A path without a wildcard is removed from every edge; the wildcard only widens the set of paths.

choices.text: Their browsers kept a copy of their own
choices.why: Right. An invalidation clears CloudFront's caches only. A versioned name is new to the browser too.

choices.text: The regional edge cache keeps a copy the invalidation skips
choices.why: The regional caches are CloudFront's and are cleared too.

choices.text: `COMPLETED` in AWS means queued, not done
choices.why: Queued is `InProgress`. Completed means every edge has dropped the path.

prompt: Put the steps of releasing a new stylesheet with versioned names in order.
hint: The new file has to exist before anything links to it.
items: upload it to the bucket with a year's `max-age`
publish the page that links to the new name
leave `shop.3f9a2c.css` in place for pages still cached
trap: Publishing the page before the file is uploaded is the usual slip: for a moment the page links to a name that does not exist yet.

prompt: In moto, an invalidation is `COMPLETED` the moment it is created. What does that say about AWS?
hint: Were there any edges to clear?

choices.text: That AWS also finishes invalidations instantly
choices.why: AWS's starts `InProgress` and finishes when every edge has dropped the paths.

choices.text: Nothing: moto has no edges, so there is nothing to wait for
choices.why: Right. It is the same as `INSYNC` in lesson 21: a status with nothing behind it.

choices.text: That small invalidations skip the `InProgress` state
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with moto's answer; it says the same for any path.

choices.text: That the paths were never cached, so nothing had to be removed
choices.why: That would also be true in moto, which caches nothing anywhere; it still says nothing about AWS.

prompt: At the list of 16 September 2026, what do 2,048 GB sent to viewers in South America through CloudFront cost, in dollars, counting transfer only?
hint: 0.110 a GB in the first 10 TB.

prompt: What does the shop pay for the bytes CloudFront fetches from the bucket in `sa-east-1`?
hint: A line of lesson 1's own offer.

choices.text: 0.15 a GB, the same as to the internet
choices.why: That is the price of leaving the region to the internet. To CloudFront it is a different line.

choices.text: 0.01 a GB each way, like crossing a zone
choices.why: Crossing a zone is inside the region. The fetch to CloudFront has its own line.

choices.text: Nothing: `SAE1-CloudFront-Out-Bytes` is priced at zero
choices.why: Right. The shop pays when CloudFront sends the bytes to viewers, not when it fetches them.

choices.text: 0.110 a GB, the CloudFront price for South America
choices.why: That is what the viewer's side costs. The fetch from the origin is free.

prompt: In one month the shop invalidates 2,400 paths, none of them with a wildcard. At 0.005 a path after the first 1,000, what does that cost, in dollars?
hint: Only the paths past 1,000 are billed.

prompt: To save money, a colleague moves the shop's distribution to `PriceClass_200`. Most customers are in Brazil. What happens to them?
hint: Which part of the world does the cheaper class leave out?

choices.text: Nothing changes for them; the class only affects Asia and Africa
choices.why: Price Class 200 includes Asia and Africa. South America is what it leaves out.

choices.text: They are served from edges abroad, further away
choices.why: Right. For a shop whose customers are in Brazil the saving is a slower shop.

choices.text: Their requests go straight to the origin in `sa-east-1`
choices.why: Viewers are still served by CloudFront, only from edges in the included parts of the world.

choices.text: They are refused until the class includes Brazil
choices.why: A price class never refuses anybody; geographic restriction would.

prompt: A file sold to one customer must be downloadable by that customer only, and only until Friday. Which feature fits?
hint: A link that carries its own proof and its own expiry.

choices.text: Geographic restriction to the customer's country
choices.why: A country holds millions of people; it cannot pick one customer.

choices.text: A WAF rule that allows the customer's IP address
choices.why: An address changes with the network the customer is on, and says nothing about Friday.

choices.text: A signed URL that expires on Friday
choices.why: Right. CloudFront checks the signature against the key group and refuses it after the time the shop chose.

choices.text: An invalidation of the file on Friday
choices.why: An invalidation removes a copy from the edges; anybody could still download it before and after.

prompt: The distribution has a WAF web ACL and the bucket is behind OAC. A tester still reaches the shop's load balancer directly, around every rule. What closes that?
hint: The origin has to admit only CloudFront.

choices.text: A second web ACL in `sa-east-1`, attached to the load balancer as well as the distribution
choices.why: It could filter at the ALB too, but it leaves the door to it open to the whole internet.

choices.text: An OAC on the load balancer origin
choices.why: OAC is for buckets and a few other AWS origins; it does not close a load balancer.

choices.text: Turning on `redirect-to-https`
choices.why: That changes what viewers of the distribution get, not who may reach the load balancer.

choices.text: A security group on the load balancer that admits only CloudFront's managed prefix list
choices.why: Right. Then CloudFront is the only way in, and the web ACL sees every request.

prompt: The shop's pages are different for every logged-in customer. Which behaviour fits them?
hint: A copy shared by everybody would show one customer's basket to another.

choices.text: `CachingOptimized`, so the load balancer does less work
choices.why: Keyed on the path only, every customer would get the first customer's page.

choices.text: `CachingDisabled` with `AllViewer`, forwarding the cookies
choices.why: Right. Nothing is kept, and the origin receives what it needs to know who is asking.

choices.text: `CachingOptimized` with the session cookie added to the key
choices.why: That stores a copy per customer that nobody else can use, a cache that only costs.

choices.text: No behaviour: pages cannot go through CloudFront
choices.why: They can, and the shop's do, under the default behaviour.

prompt: The shop sends 10,240 GB a month to viewers in Brazil. How many dollars a month does CloudFront's transfer save against sending the same bytes straight from `sa-east-1`, at 0.110 against 0.150?
hint: The difference per GB, times the GB.

prompt: Match each need to the CloudFront feature that meets it.
hint: Four features of the lesson, and one left over.

pairs.left: keep the bucket private and still serve its files
make edges forget a file published by mistake
refuse viewers from a country the licence excludes
rate-limit an address hammering the checkout
